title: Paying Parents to Watch their Babies
author: Other Feminisms
summary: Other Feminisms examines a rumored federal proposal to let parents themselves count as paid childcare providers, arguing that whatever its legal and funding complications, the underlying idea deserves support: parents are frequently told the government wants to help them by paying for anyone but them to watch their own baby. Drawing on the lapsed state-level 'At Home Infant Care' pilots and international comparisons, the piece argues most countries with strong public childcare pair it with direct payments to parents who stay home, partly from economic necessity, since infant care ratios make center-based care unprofitable at the youngest ages. The author proposes exempting one parent from federal work requirements for a child's first six to twelve months as a more workable version of the idea, treating infant caregiving like school enrollment.
points: Argues policy debates treat parental care of infants as suspect while readily subsidizing professional providers to do the same work.
Revives 'At Home Infant Care,' a lapsed 1990s-2000s state pilot that paid parents directly, as a workable federal model.
Notes that Nordic countries pair universal childcare with direct payments to at-home parents partly for economic reasons: infant ratios make center care unprofitable without cross-subsidy.
Proposes exempting one parent from federal work requirements for a baby's first six to twelve months, akin to school enrollment.
quotes: it's hard for parents of young children to be told the government is eager to support them in having anyone but their baby's parents watch their baby.

Instead of having states cover the cost, the federal government could exempt one parent in a household from CCDF's work requirement for the first six months to a year of their baby's life. Caring for an infant would be treated the way being enrolled in school is, an investment in the family's future.
It's not "traddiness" that leads the Nordics to pay stay at home parents of young babies. It's partly responsiveness to parents' desires, and it's partly simple economic practicalities.
Infants are very very expensive to include in professional child care settings. They need very low caregiver to infant ratios.

Allowing parents of babies to care for them directly, as they most frequently desire, would mean the government was supporting the natural family, not forcing parents to contract out the care that matters most.
